news.title: Where Is the Socialist Wave Really Coming From?
news.text:
I’ve said before that primary wins of DSA candidates over establishment Democrats reflect where the Democrat Party is already headed ideologically. But until the midterm elections are over, Democrats are going to try very hard to publicly distance themselves from the DSA.

What are they trying to hide? Well, it’s obvious. What the establishment doesn’t want the public to understand is that the socialist insurgency isn’t an insurgency at all. It is coming from within the party's own base.

In fact, it’s so obvious that even CNN can see what’s going on.

CNN's chief data analyst, Harry Enten, laid out exactly what’s happening. "I think there's this idea, perhaps in Democratic circles, 'Oh, they're coming in from the outside.' No, no, the call is coming from inside the house. It's your own voters." Enten had the numbers to back him up. He pointed out that 41% of self-identified Democrat voters now identify as democratic socialists, compared with just 20% of independents who lean Democrat. "These are Democratic voters," Enten said. "These are people who voted for Kamala Harris."

CNN's Harry Enten on the rise of Democrat socialists across the country:"We‘ve seen those Democratic socialists really thrive in big urban areas, right? New York, Pennsylvania. You go out to Colorado. Well, it‘s no longer just in the urban areas anymore..." pic.twitter.com/NZIPHHbfDl— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) July 31, 2026

The polling confirms this is no longer a fringe phenomenon. A Fox News poll found recently that 52% of Democrats now hold a favorable view of socialism, compared with 43% who view it unfavorably. A majority of Democrat voters, not a rebellious minority, now embrace socialism outright. Gallup polling cited by CNN found the number even higher: 66% of Democrats hold a positive view of socialism. Different pollsters. Different methodologies. Same conclusion.

HARRY ENTEN: "The call is coming from inside the house…these are Democratic voters; these are people who voted for Kamala Harris…more than 2 in 5 Democratic voters who identify as Democratic Socialists." pic.twitter.com/0IQKG54fZm— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) July 31, 2026

The socialist wave in the Democrat Party is happening everywhere, not just the bluest cities in the bluest states. Enten pointed to the Wisconsin Democrat primary, where a candidate named Francesca Hong has emerged as the runaway favorite for the nomination. "She's a Democratic socialist," Enten said. "Her chance is up like a rocket ... 96% chance to be the Democratic nominee in Wisconsin, a Democratic socialist, according to the Cash Prediction markets." Enten didn't stop there. "So this is not just happening now in New York, Philadelphia, Denver," he said. "It looks to me like it's going to be happening in a place like Wisconsin, which, of course, is a very purple state."

Recommended: Here’s What Democrats Don’t Want You to Know About the Fauci Investigation

Enten's analysis is a warning sign for Democrats. It shows how deep this socialist problem really runs, and it makes the party's leftward drift obvious to anyone watching. This creates a real problem heading into the midterms. The same Fox News poll that found a majority of Democrats embracing socialism found the opposite result among the broader electorate: just 17% of all voters view socialism favorably, while 77% view it unfavorably. Voters overwhelmingly reject socialism everywhere outside the Democrat Party's own coalition.

Democrat strategists can keep telling themselves this is a containable outside insurgency confined to a few safe seats. But it’s widespread, and in the end, it’s Democrat Party voters who are pulling the levers for these candidates. They are making the choice. And when the general election season heats up, you can bet the Republicans are going to use this to their advantage.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: World News | Trump Blames Minnesota Governor, Not Iran, for Cyberattacks on State's Water Systems
news.text:
Washington DC [US], August 1 (ANI): US President Donald Trump has dismissed reports attributing a recent cyberattack on Minnesota's water infrastructure to Iran, placing the blame instead on state leadership and Democratic Governor Tim Walz.

Speaking at a Cabinet meeting at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, Trump rejected findings by intelligence agencies and state authorities.

"I just want to mention that we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran," Trump said. "I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent."

He further questioned Tehran's involvement, referencing the broader geopolitical climate. "There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, 'Oh, it's Iran.' Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota," Trump added.

Also Read | Qualcomm Price Hike: Chipmaker Officially Announces Broad Price Increases Amid Component Shortages.

The President's remarks come amidst an ongoing military conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran, as well as his long-standing scepticism towards the US intelligence community.

Trump's stance directly contradicts preliminary assessments shared by US and state officials. Officials familiar with the incident informed The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the breach.

Responding to the allegations on social platform X, Governor Tim Walz criticised the President's stance on the critical infrastructure breach.

"Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there's no plan to win a war with Iran," Walz posted.

The exchange highlights escalating political friction between the Trump administration and Minnesota authorities. Tensions intensified earlier this year following the killing of two US citizens by immigration agents during street demonstrations, alongside political clashes over state-administered social services programmes.

Walz, who was Vice President Kamala Harris' running mate in the 2024 election won by Trump and JD Vance, abandoned his bid for a third gubernatorial term in January amid scrutiny over programme oversight, though he has not been accused of personal wrongdoing.

Federal agencies had previously issued warnings that Iranian-affiliated actors were actively targeting computerised controls across water facilities, power networks, and local governments to cause domestic disruption, Fox News reported.

On the ground, state agency Minnesota IT Services confirmed that a "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems". However, state authorities maintained that the investigation remains active and has not yet formally named a "specific actor".

The incident impacted local infrastructure across several municipalities, with malicious software temporarily shutting down digital controls for a well and water treatment plant in Braham, while Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted operations to manual control, according to Fox News.

Despite the disruption to automated systems, the Minnesota Department of Health confirmed that it is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage", verifying that there is no known threat to drinking water supplies.

Iranian cyber operations have previously targeted US infrastructure. In 2023, hackers affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps breached programmable controllers at several US water and wastewater facilities by exploiting default credentials, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

In another case, the US Department of Justice charged an Iranian hacker with unlawfully accessing the control system of a dam in Rye, New York, in 2013. (ANI)

ANI brings the latest news on Politics and Current Affairs in India & around the World, Sports, Health, Fitness, Entertainment, & News. news.title: ANDREW NEIL: If you want to know why socialism is on the march in America, look at the medieval kleptocracy that is the First Family
news.text:
It was inevitable that, at some stage, America’s populist Left would try to do to the Democratic Party what the populist Right has already done to the Republican Party: take it over.

Maybe now is the time their dreams will come true. Their chosen vehicle for the takeover bid is an organisation called Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

The DSA may have been around for almost 50 years, but throughout its existence it has been a political irrelevance. ‘Socialism’ has always been something of a dirty word in US politics, too akin to communism, too redolent of the old world (Europe).

Mainstream Democrats have always shunned it. Yet, remarkably, it is now part of the US political lexicon as never before.

The DSA has burgeoned since Donald Trump was re-elected in 2024. With more than 120,000 members – a majority of them new recruits – plus many tens of thousands more who regard themselves as ‘DSA adjacent’, it is now the largest explicitly socialist movement in American history. It’s not a third party. It contests Democratic primaries, which choose the party’s candidates, backing upstart radicals against old, complacent incumbents.

Its $9million annual budget is peanuts by US political standards but it can count on an army of activists and it has already scored some remarkable successes. The DSA concentrates its efforts on heavily Democratic areas where, if you win the party’s primary nomination, you’re a shoo-in come the real election.

Its poster boy, of course, is Zohran Mamdani, the young, charismatic, self-styled socialist who won last year’s Democratic primary for mayor of New York, which he duly became in January.

Mamdani is to DSA what Trump is to MAGA: its most famous face and champion. Three Mamdani-backed radicals have recently ousted incumbent Democrats in New York congressional primaries for safe seats. This means, inevitably, they’ll be in the next House of Representatives.

Mainstream Democrats have been quick to claim the DSA’s appeal is limited to the liberal elites of America’s coastal cities. But its candidates have also won primaries in places far away from the coast, including Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, North Carolina, Vermont and Utah. It claims almost 40 wins, so far, in various primaries for both state and federal elections.

Its biggest test comes on Tuesday in, of all places, Michigan, a no-nonsense, mid-western, blue-collar state which voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024 (but only just, both times).

The incumbent Democratic senator has decided not to run again. So the primary is a straight fight between a rather run-of-the-mill mainstream Democratic congresswoman, Haley Stevens, and Abdul El-Sayed, rising star of the DSA-aligned Democrats.

El-Sayed is a classic case of America’s new breed of socialist. The son of an Egyptian immigrant engineer, he’s a Muslim who was brought up in an affluent Detroit suburb.

After winning a full scholarship to study medicine at the University of Michigan, he received a prestigious Rhodes Scholarship to attend Oriel College, Oxford, where he captained the lacrosse team. He then completed his medical studies at Columbia, one of the select group of Ivy League universities.

So we’re not talking about some horny-handed son of toil here. But then it has been a long time since the Democrats were the party of America’s working class. Today’s Democratic Party base is white-collar, educated, middle-class, metropolitan – and generally unhappy with life.

Education levels are now the best predictor of how Americans will vote. In 2024, Trump won 29 of the 30 states with the lowest share of university graduates. His Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris (remember her?), won 14 of the 15 states with the highest share of university graduates.

There’s an added twist to explain the DSA’s growing popularity. Rather than dwelling on the perceived exploitation of the workers – the traditional Marxist pitch – today’s US socialists appeal to the grievances of the young, educated metropolitan classes whose liberal arts degrees have not equipped them for careers at a time when artificial intelligence is gobbling up so many entry-level jobs.

Though from affluent backgrounds, they do not feel well off themselves. Poor salaries, high housing costs and sticky inflation have seen to that.

A downwardly mobile life beckons, and that scares them. It is on such sentiments that modern US socialism preys. Solutions are another matter. The DSA can make our own loony Left sound quite sensible.

Its online manifesto calls for the destruction of the ‘capitalist oligarchy’ and a ‘socialist future’, the abolition of prisons and police, the defunding of the US military and closure of all overseas bases, a 32-hour working week (with no pay cuts, of course), universal free housing, rent controls (why would they be needed if housing was free?), public ownership of ‘essential industries’ and the ‘largest corporations’, and an end to border controls.

Plus the ripping apart of the US constitution. The Senate would be abolished, as would the Presidency and the Supreme Court, to be replaced by an executive and judiciary under the control of the House of Representatives – a sort of new ‘people’s parliament’.

Michigan’s El-Sayed is trying not to run on any of this. After all, he wants to beat not just the Democratic opponents in the primary but his Republican candidate come November.

He still has a lot of explaining to do. When riots raged in US cities after the death of George Floyd in 2020 he said the police should be defunded (he now says he was just using the language that was ‘in vogue’ at the time).

He also once described a moderate Democratic senator as ‘an ogre’ whose head he’d like to put ‘on a pike’ to intimidate other moderates.

He’s also cosied up to Hasan Piker, a notorious hard-Leftist who has opined that ‘America deserved 9/11’ and described Chairman Mao, the Chinese despot whose policies killed more than 40million, as ‘one of the great leaders of this world’.

Piker is also pro-Hamas. El-Sayed may not be that. But he calls Israel a ‘rogue state’, accuses it of ‘genocide’ and wants the US to ban further arms sales to it. This is significant. Deep hostility to Israel, often spilling into outright anti-Semitism, is in the DNA of DSA activists. Whatever policy disagreements they may have, a loathing of Israel unites them.

Just as a previous generation of young people was radicalised by the Vietnam War, so the DSA has been radicalised by Israel’s response in Gaza to the Hamas atrocities of October 7. It is what really fires them up, far more than any domestic agenda.

Republicans see a ‘Get out of jail free’ card here. If the shrill, extreme voice of the DSA is increasingly the voice of the Democrats, then perhaps November’s midterms won’t be quite the bloodbath for Trump and his party they fear. Well, maybe. But three polls this week all put Trump’s approval below 35 per cent, an all-time low.

More than 70 per cent think he’s handling the economy (the number one issue) badly and almost 75 per cent disapprove of his flailing war on Iran. Republican voter morale has slumped. Many have indicated they just won’t bother to vote come November.

The Democrats, of course, are not in much better shape. Their approval rating is as low as Trump’s. The party is still run by a gerontocracy that hasn’t had an original idea or candidate with widespread appeal for years. At least the DSA is clearing out the dead wood, at last. Even moderate Democrats acknowledge that.

US socialism still has some way to go before it becomes mainstream, if it ever does. But voters increasingly disillusioned with Trump and mainstream Democrats could easily look past their daft ideas and give them their votes – just for the hell of it.

In a sense, it’s hard to blame them. Traditional Democrats have run out of steam and purpose. Trump has started another forever war of the sort he was elected to avoid. People see him, rightly, as indifferent to the crippling cost-of-living crisis ordinary families are enduring.

Meanwhile, the kleptocracy that is the First Family and their hangers on stuff their own pockets with a level of greed that would shame a medieval monarch. If you wonder why socialism, of all things, is suddenly on the march in America – that’s the answer.

news.title: Kamala Harris teases potential 2028 platform: ‘I know this is going to be controversial’
news.text:
Kamala Harris on Friday signaled she’d support abolishing the Electoral College and packing the Supreme Court – an indication that the former vice president has moved further to the left since her disastrous 2024 presidential campaign. 

“I know this is going to be controversial coming from me, in particular,” Harris said in remarks at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville, Tenn., before laying out part of her potential 2028 platform. 

“We need to revisit the Electoral College. We need to revisit the point of expanding the court, to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts. We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C.,” the former vice president argued. 

Abolishing the Electoral College – a plank on the Democratic Socialists of America platform – is not a position Harris held during her failed 2024 presidential campaign. Harris lost both the Electoral College and popular vote to President Trump that year. 

Similarly, Harris didn’t back court packing in 2024. The former vice president instead favored term limits and subjecting justices to a binding code of ethics. 

Harris supported statehood for Washington, DC, during her campaign against Trump, but not for Puerto Rico.

In her remarks, the former vice president also called for “accountability and consequences” for federal judicial nominees that intentionally mislead the Senate Judiciary Committee, including putting in place rules that would allow the panel to hold nominees who lie in contempt of Congress. 

Harris’ leftward tilt comes amid reports she’s been talking to prominent progressives, including socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, ahead of another possible run at the White House. 

Harris reached out to Mamdani in June to discuss the future of the Democratic Party and set up a longer conversation, according to Axios. 

In April, the former vice president met with DSA darling Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) in Chicago, the outlet reported.

Harris is currently the front-runner for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. 

She leads California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Ocasio-Cortez by double-digits, according to the latest RealClearPolitics average of early polls.

In her remarks in Nashville, Harris did not rule out another White House run, telling conference attendees that she has “not made a decision.” 

“I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms,” she said.

news.title: Cook Political Report Finds Fewer Competitive House Districts After Redistricting
news.text:
The report tracks how each of the 435 House districts votes for president compared with the country as a whole, a measure it calls the Partisan Voter Index. A district that voted 5 points more Republican than the national average is scored R+5. One that voted 8 points more Democratic is scored D+8. Districts within 5 points of the national average in either direction are the ones both parties usually have a real chance of winning.

That group shrank this year. Ten states redrew their congressional maps ahead of the midterms, and afterward the number of districts in that competitive range fell from 87 to 77.

Because there are fewer of them, Democrats have to win a larger share. The report calculated that if each party carries the districts that strongly favor it, Democrats would need 57 of the 77 competitive seats, or about 74 percent, to reach the 218 needed for a majority. Under the old maps, they would have needed 59 of 87, or 68 percent.

The typical district also became more Republican-leaning. After the 2024 election, the middle district in the country was California’s 22nd, held by Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.), which voted about half a point more Republican than the nation. Under the new maps, the middle district is Pennsylvania’s 10th, held by Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), which votes about 2.5 points more Republican.

Analyst David Wasserman, who wrote the report, said that puts the map roughly where it was between 2012 and 2017, and described it as “more skewed towards Republicans and less elastic than before.”

Wasserman offered a hypothetical to show the size of the change. If Democrats won every district that leans less than 3 points Republican and nothing more, they would have ended up with 235 seats under the old maps. Under the new ones, the same performance would produce 223—both still constituting a majority and a change in control for the House.

Florida, Missouri, and Texas accounted for three-quarters of the increase in strongly Republican districts. California accounted for more than half of the national drop in competitive ones, cutting its own number of swing districts from 12 to six. Wasserman attributed the difference to California Democrats replacing a map drawn by an independent commission with a more favorable one, while Republicans in the other three states redrew maps that were already favorable in their direction.

He also wrote that Republicans fell short of the 10 to 12 seats their strategists initially expected to gain, and that Democrats remain favored to win the House this year. Picking up districts that lean 3 to 5 points Republican is realistic in a strong midterm year for the party out of power, he wrote, but the new maps lower how many seats Democrats can gain overall.

The Crystal Ball revised 13 of its race ratings that day, raising the number of contests it considers a coin flip from 15 to 20. That is a separate measure from Cook’s.

Cook is describing how districts lean over time, no matter who runs in them. The Crystal Ball is predicting who wins this November, which takes into account the candidates, their fundraising, and the national mood. A map with fewer naturally competitive districts can still produce more close races in a given year.

Kondik wrote that he made the changes to bring the ratings in line with a view he already held, that Democrats are favored. The revision left 208 districts rated at least leaning Republican and 207 at least leaning Democratic. He put his best estimate at a Democratic majority in the low-to-mid 220s and wrote that Republicans still have a path to keeping control.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee sent out the ratings changes the same day, saying the map continues to move in its favor with fewer than 100 days until the election.

“All of the momentum is behind Democrats in the fight for the House,” DCCC spokesman Viet Shelton said, adding that the committee’s candidates are running on an affordability message.

The National Republican Congressional Committee cited the Cook analysis in its response. In a statement to The Epoch Times, national press secretary Mike Marinella said Republicans are running on a more favorable map, record fundraising, and stronger candidates, and said Democratic nominees and policies leave “their path to the majority far more challenging than the pundits suggest.”

news.title: Cook Political Report Finds Fewer Competitive House Districts After Redistricting
news.text:
The report tracks how each of the 435 House districts votes for president compared with the country as a whole, a measure it calls the Partisan Voter Index. A district that voted 5 points more Republican than the national average is scored R+5. One that voted 8 points more Democratic is scored D+8. Districts within 5 points of the national average in either direction are the ones both parties usually have a real chance of winning.

That group shrank this year. Ten states redrew their congressional maps ahead of the midterms, and afterward the number of districts in that competitive range fell from 87 to 77.

Because there are fewer of them, Democrats have to win a larger share. The report calculated that if each party carries the districts that strongly favor it, Democrats would need 57 of the 77 competitive seats, or about 74 percent, to reach the 218 needed for a majority. Under the old maps, they would have needed 59 of 87, or 68 percent.

The typical district also became more Republican-leaning. After the 2024 election, the middle district in the country was California’s 22nd, held by Rep. David Valadao (R-Calif.), which voted about half a point more Republican than the nation. Under the new maps, the middle district is Pennsylvania’s 10th, held by Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), which votes about 2.5 points more Republican.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Just Shared Tax Returns—Net Worth Compared to Other Governors
news.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom on Friday released more than 700 pages of tax returns spanning four years as his finances remain under scrutiny from President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice. Newsom, a Democrat, announced in June that he was under investigation by the DOJ and that federal agents had been seeking documents and records. He framed the move as retaliation tied to his potential presidential ambitions, and one of the investigations centers on Newsom’s wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, and her taxes. Newsweek reached out to Newsom’s team for comment via email. What Tax Returns Reveal About Gavin Newsom's Finances The tax returns revealed that Newsom and his wife made between $1.7 million and $2 million annually from 2022 through 2024 and that they paid about half a million each year in taxes. Tax returns for 2025 were not released because the couple filed for an extension. That indicates that little has changed since he became governor in 2019, when they reported an annual income of $1.7 million. In 2021, they sold a home for nearly $6 million, making about $800,000; that year, they made $4.2 million and paid over $1 million in taxes. They also earned about $2 million in 2022. The California governor receives a salary of $245,929 as of 2025; the office receives an annual raise, and the salary was 209,747 when he took office, according to the California Department of Human Resources. Much of his income, however, comes from businesses he managed before becoming governor. Prior to entering politics, Newsom founded the PlumpJack Group alongside his friend Gordon Getty, which would eventually manage more than 20 businesses including wineries, liquor stores, bars and restaurants. After being elected governor, Newsom said he would put the business in a blind trust. The company is now run by his sister and cousin. Jennifer Siebel Newsom, meanwhile, reported that she lost money from her production company, Girls Club Entertainment. Gavin Newsom's Net Worth Newsom’s precise net worth has not been made public, but estimates from Finance Monthly have put it around $30 million. His net worth includes the portfolio from the PlumpJack Group, as well as his real estate properties. Newsom bought a $9 million home in 2024 outside of San Francisco, The San Francisco Standard reported. He also owns a home near Sacramento that he purchased for $3.7 million in 2019. Several other governors have higher estimated net worths. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker is seen as the wealthiest governor, with an estimated net worth of $3.9 billion, according to Forbes. Several other governors are estimated to have a net worth of more than $100 million. That includes Democratic Colorado Governor Jared Polis, who has an estimated net worth of $400 million, per The Denver Gazette. Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont is viewed as among the wealthier governors, having reported an income of $54 million in 2022, according to CT Mirror. His wife, Annie Lamont, has a net worth of $650 million, according to Forbes. Other governors have a more modest net worth. Governor Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, viewed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, has an estimated net worth of around $100,000, according to Celebrity Net Worth. Bridge Michigan reported in 2024 that Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer was worth around $2.3 million. C BS News reported that Florida GOP Governor Ron DeSantis has a net worth of around $2 million. Gavin Newsom Investigation: Why Trump DOJ Is Probing California Governor The release of Newsom’s tax returns comes more than a month after the governor first confirmed that he is under investigation. On June 15, Newsom said federal agents in recent days have visited the homes of family members, friends and former employees seeking documents and records. He said Trump is “coming after me because I am considering running for President,” while portraying the investigation as politically motivated and unprecedented. A source familiar with the situation previously told Newsweek that several investigations have been ongoing for about a year. The investigations originated in California from whistleblowers and local sources. They are being run through the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Sacramento. One of the investigations deals with Newsom’s wife and her taxes. Another deals with a former chief of staff and potentially current staffers, but more details about the scope of that investigation remained private. Newsom said the DOJ investigation also involves his wife, Jennifer, but the nature of the alleged probe is unclear. He said the DOJ is “abusing the grand jury process” in its demands for records. Newsom Is Potential 2028 Candidate The California governor has also been frequently named as a potential candidate for Democrats in the 2028 presidential race, though he has not formally said he plans to run. The latest polls show Newsom as a leading candidate among the potential field. A McLaughlin & Associates poll, which surveyed 472 likely voters from July 15-21, showed former Vice President Kamala Harris leading with 28 percent, but Newsom followed at 17 percent. New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez followed at 10 percent, while 8 percent said they would vote for former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. An Emerson College poll showed Buttigieg leading at 19 percent, while Newsom followed at 17 percent. Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff received 13 percent support, while Harris received 8 percent in that poll. It surveyed 574 likely voters from July 19-20, 2026. Newsom told reporters earlier in July that whether he joins the race would be determined by “fate.” “I really believe it’s fate,” he said. “You meet the moment, you represent something where you can uniquely and distinctively make the case that your voice matters in a competitive field where there will be stadiums full of Democrats. Every conceivable stripe of Democrat will be on display.” This article includes reporting by the Associated Press. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Sam Wilson.

 Trump and far-right seize on Spanish migration crisis 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — US President Donald Trump led far-right attempts Friday on both sides of the Atlantic to make political capital from Spain’s migration crisis, portraying the migrant surge in Ceuta as a warning for America if his opponents get into power.

“It’s terrible. Remember that picture. That’s going to be us in three years if the wrong side gets in,” Trump was quoted as saying by Fox News. “If the Democrats get in, you will not live a very good life.”

With polls showing Trump’s support has fallen into the low 30 percent range and opposition Democrats hoping to win at least partial control of Congress in November midterm elections, the crisis in Spain offers Republicans a chance to return to one of their political strongpoints.

News footage of migrants overwhelming barriers to get into Ceuta — a tiny Spanish territory on the Moroccan coast — aired repeatedly on Fox News and went viral across right-wing Trump-allied social media accounts.

In Europe, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel claimed in an X post that “Ceuta was left in ruins overnight” by the mass influx from Morocco.

She argued that Germany is “likely the destination for most of these migrants.”

“Germany must prepare itself: borders must be secured and rejections rigorously enforced,” wrote Weidel, whose party is backed by top Trump officials.

Both Italy’s right-wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni and the populist right-wing ruling coalition in Finland called for excluding Spain from the European visa-free zone as a result of the situation.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a billionaire Trump supporter, said the Ceuta situation was caused by Spain’s policy of offering hundreds of thousands of migrants already in the country a legal status.

“They are replacing Spaniards with migrants,” Babis said.

– ‘Invasion of the West’ –

Trump’s election victory over Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 was fueled by voter worries over uncontrolled migration on the US-Mexico border and his lurid warnings of migrants coming to murder Americans and even to eat their pets.

Trump’s vice president, JD Vance, posted news footage on Friday of migrants pouring into Ceuta on X and wrote it highlighted “radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West.”

“These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration,” Vance posted on X.

Late Thursday, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a chief architect of Trump’s anti-migration crackdown, posted video of the Ceuta crisis and said “Democrats will see your home trampled and stolen by invaders and they will rejoice.”

Officials familiar with the incident informed The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the breach.Responding to the allegations on social platform X, Governor Tim Walz criticised the President's stance on the critical infrastructure breach.

"Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there's no plan to win a war with Iran," Walz posted.The exchange highlights escalating political friction between the Trump administration and Minnesota authorities. However, state authorities maintained that the investigation remains active and has not yet formally named a "specific actor".The incident impacted local infrastructure across several municipalities, with malicious software temporarily shutting down digital controls for a well and water treatment plant in Braham, while Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted operations to manual control, according to Fox News.Despite the disruption to automated systems, the Minnesota Department of Health confirmed that it is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage", verifying that there is no known threat to drinking water supplies.Iranian cyber operations have previously targeted US infrastructure. In 2023, hackers affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps breached programmable controllers at several US water and wastewater facilities by exploiting default credentials, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.In another case, the US Department of Justice charged an Iranian hacker with unlawfully accessing the control system of a dam in Rye, New York, in 2013. news.title: Trump blames Minnesota and Gov. Tim Walz for cyberattack that feds have traced to Iran
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday renewed an on-again, off-again feud with one of his 2024 election opponents by suggesting that an Iranian cyberattack against Minnesota’s water infrastructure was due to the state government’s incompetence rather than Tehran’s malfeasance.

Trump was speaking during a cabinet meeting at Camp David in Thurmont, Maryland when, unprompted, he downplayed an advisory from both the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Environmental Protection Agency, which had warned that Iranian hackers have been targeting water and sewage systems and other critical infrastructure sectors across the United States.

"Today, I just want to mention that we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran. I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent. There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota,” Trump said.

“They like to say, ‘Oh, it was Iran’ — Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

The announcement from the federal agencies advised that “malicious cyber actors” were targeting water system infrastructure, and a separate alert from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned that some attacks had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations.”

Tehran is known to have invested heavily in hybrid capabilities such as cyber warfare, and water facilities are often targets of such attacks because their digital operations are often under resourced in terms of financing or personnel needed to maintain the latest security patches on software. 

But rather than acknowledge the threat, Trump chose instead to lash out at the North Star State’s Democratic governor, Tim Walz.

Walz, who earlier this year announced he would not run for re-election after right-wing media figures heaped blame on him for alleged government benefits fraud committed by Somali-Americans living in his state, was the running-mate of former vice president Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election. 

His frosty relationship with Trump dates back to four years before that, when his state was the epicenter of racial justice protests sparked by the murder of a Blackman, George Floyd, by a Minneapolis, Minnesota police officer. 

Trump’s rejection of the FBI’s warnings about Iranian hackers isn’t the first time he’s shot down his own administration’s conclusions about a foreign adversary. 

For nearly a decade, Trump has denied that Russia interfered in the 2016 election on his behalf despite U.S. Intelligence Community assessments that Moscow had been behind both a hack-and-leak operation targeting the Democratic National Committee and Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign as well as a massive social media trolling operation meant to boost him and denigrate Clinton, who he defeated to win his first term nine years ago. 

During a now-infamous 2017 press conference alongside Russian president Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump said he took Putin at his word after the Russian leader denied having meddled in the previous year’s election.

"President Putin says it's not Russia. I don't see any reason why it would be," he said, adding that the Russian leader had been “extremely strong and powerful in his denial.”

And when pressed further on whether he believed his administration’s assessment about the Iranian cyberattacks on Friday, Trump doubled down on his previous attack agains Walz.

“You know who's behind it? Minnesota, because they're grossly incompetent. I think the governor's behind it. I don't think there was an Iranian cyberattack,” he said.
news.summary: Trump has a history of downplaying U.S. intelligence community conclusions when it benefits him politically

The announcement from the federal agencies advised that "malicious cyber actors" were targeting water system infrastructure, and a separate alert from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned that some attacks had "resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations."

Tehran is known to have invested heavily in hybrid capabilities such as cyber warfare, and water facilities are often targets of such attacks because their digital operations are often under resourced in terms of financing or personnel needed to maintain the latest security patches on software.

But rather than acknowledge the threat, Trump chose instead to lash out at the North Star State's Democratic governor, Tim Walz.

Walz, who earlier this year announced he would not run for re-election after right-wing media figures heaped blame on him for alleged government benefits fraud committed by Somali-Americans living in his state, was the running-mate of former vice president Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election.

His frosty relationship with Trump dates back to four years before that, when his state was the epicenter of racial justice protests sparked by the murder of a Blackman, George Floyd, by a Minneapolis, Minnesota police officer.

Trump's rejection of the FBI's warnings about Iranian hackers isn't the first time he's shot down his own administration's conclusions about a foreign adversary.

For nearly a decade, Trump has denied that Russia interfered in the 2016 election on his behalf despite U.S. Intelligence Community assessments that Moscow had been behind both a hack-and-leak operation targeting the Democratic National Committee and Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign as well as a massive social media trolling operation meant to boost him and denigrate Clinton, who he defeated to win his first term nine years ago.

During a now-infamous 2017 press conference alongside Russian president Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump said he took Putin at his word after the Russian leader denied having meddled in the previous year's election.

"President Putin says it's not Russia. I don't see any reason why it would be," he said, adding that the Russian leader had been "extremely strong and powerful in his denial."

And when pressed further on whether he believed his administration's assessment about the Iranian cyberattacks on Friday, Trump doubled down on his previous attack agains Walz.

"You know who's behind it? Minnesota, because they're grossly incompetent. I think the governor's behind it. I don't think there was an Iranian cyberattack," he said.

news.title: WNBA Star Brittney Griner and Wife Cherelle Griner’s Relationship Timeline
news.text:
Love and basketball. Brittney Griner is one of the best athletes in the WNBA — and she always has her sweetheart, Cherelle Griner, cheering her on from the sidelines.
The Olympic gold medalist and the teacher met as undergraduates at Baylor University in Texas while Brittney was making a name for herself as one of the best college basketball players of all time. They didn't start dating until years later, however, when they reconnected after the athlete split from her first wife, Glory Johnson.
"I will never forget the day I met you at Baylor in the sub area!" Brittney wrote via Instagram in June 2020. "You tapped me on my shoulder and told me I took your milkshake (still up for debate lol) and I was immediately blown away at your beauty! You had no idea but I knew you were the one for me baby. You stuck by my side at the lowest and at the highest!"
The Phoenix Mercury center proposed to Cherelle in August 2018, and the duo tied the knot nearly one year later. Since then, the pair have repeatedly gushed over each other on social media, sharing snaps from vacations and commemorating their relationship milestones.
"Everyday with you is spectacular but when I get to celebrate your life and all that you are is just breathtaking ❤️!" Brittney wrote via Instagram in July 2020 to celebrate her spouse's birthday. "To many more my love."
In 2022, the couple became the subject of international news when the basketball star was detained in Russia on drug charges. Brittney was in the country playing with the EuroLeague team UMMC Ekaterinburg during the WNBA offseason.
By the time the news broke in the United States in March 2022, Brittney had already been detained for two weeks. Officials were initially worried that an aggressive response could hurt her chances of a safe return amid Russia's conflict with Ukraine, but in May 2022, the U.S. State Department said that Russia had "wrongfully detained" the Texas native.
"It’s an absolutely unimaginable situation for for BG," WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert told Time after the State Department's reclassification. "There’s not a day that goes by that I’m not working on this in some way. It was a really positive development for her case to be transferred into the part of the State Department that’s called the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs. When you get this designation of being detained, not under the best conditions, they’ve shown success at getting people out."
Cherelle, for her part, supported her wife from afar, sharing videos on social media of Brittney's time on the court. "Thank you to everyone who has reached out to me regarding my wife’s safe return from Russia," she wrote via Instagram in March 2022. "Your prayers and support are greatly appreciated. I love my wife wholeheartedly, so this message comes during one of the weakest moments of my life."
In December 2022, Cherelle was a beaming sight at the White House as President Joe Biden announced that her wife had been released from Russian custody.
"After months of being unjustly detained in Russia, held under intolerable circumstances, Brittney will soon be back in the arms of her loved ones and she should have been there all along," Biden said during a press release as Cherelle and Vice President Kamala Harris stood beside him.
"This is a day we've worked towards for a long time. We never stopped pushing for her release," he added.

news.title: Trump Claims Minnesota Is Behind Cyberattack on Its Own Water Systems, Not Iran
news.text:
President Donald Trump says Iran wasn’t behind recent cyberattacks against dozens of water systems in Minnesota. Who is really to blame? Minnesota itself, according to the whiny 80-year-old leader. The governor of Minnesota pointed out how absurd that claim was Friday while noting that DOGE cuts meant state experts had to investigate the attacks themselves without sufficient federal support.

State officials in Minnesota told the New York Times this week that attacks on 36 municipal water systems had possibly come from hackers aligned with Iran. The officials cautioned that Iran hadn’t been definitively determined to be the source of the attacks and that more data would need to be examined.

The water systems had been breached without a ransom demand and focused on disruption rather than financial gain, which has led investigators to believe the attacks are state-backed. Early reports indicate the water is still safe to drink.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published an advisory in April that warned pro-Iranian hackers were targeting U.S. energy and water infrastructure in retaliation for Trump’s war against Iran, which started Feb. 28.

Trump first talked about the cyberattacks unprompted on Friday during a publicly televised cabinet meeting from Camp David.

“We heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack and they blame it on Iran,” said Trump. “I don’t think so. I blame it on Minnesota because they’re grossly incompetent.” Trump has publicly feuded with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who ran for Vice President with Kamala Harris on the 2024 Democratic presidential ticket.

“There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants,” continued Trump. “And I would blame it on Minnesota and the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘ooh it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota.”

Trump went on with his cabinet meeting, with men like Marco Rubio talking about how the Big Boy President is doing such an amazing job. But when a handful of reporters eventually got to ask some questions at the end, Trump was asked about his incendiary comments about Minnesota.

“Can you rule out that Iran is behind the water attacks?” one reporter asked.

This time Trump went a step further, directly blaming Minnesota for apparently attacking itself:

It’s an absolutely ridiculous accusation, of course. And it’s the kind of thing that in any other era would be roundly condemned and become the focus of national media attention for days if not weeks.

The first breach of Minnesota’s systems was detected last Sunday, according to the New York Times, but it’s far from the first state to see cyber intrusions possibly linked to Iran during this war. The FBI and EPA released a warning on Thursday that at least seven states have had their water systems hacked, though the agencies didn’t name the states.

Gov. Walz tweeted in response to Trump’s wild accusations, pointing out that other states outside Minnesota have been impacted as well.

“Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too,” wrote Walz. “This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran.”

Walz also noted that DOGE, the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, had decimated the ability of the federal government to investigate these cyberattacks. “DOGE took an axe to CISA and left the U.S. exposed to cyber attacks,” wrote Walz. “Thankfully, our experts in Minnesota were able to identify the vulnerability quickly and work with local communities to stop it.”

CISA lost roughly a third of its workforce thanks to Elon Musk’s DOGE project, which has crippled the federal workforce and made the U.S. less able to respond to threats on everything from food safety to state-sponsored cyberattacks.

 DOGE took an axe to CISA and left the U.S. exposed to cyber attacks. Thankfully, our experts in Minnesota were able to identify the vulnerability quickly and work with local communities to stop it. — Governor Tim Walz (@GovTimWalz) July 31, 2026

Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. already won the war against Iran. But it’s never been clearer that he started a new war with no easy exit. If the U.S. leaves now, it effectively gives Iran control of the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of the world’s oil passes. If the U.S. continues to bomb Iran in perpetuity, it depletes its munitions supply, making America less prepared for a potential war with a near-peer adversary like China.

Trump started a war he may have “won” militarily, but he lost strategically the moment he dropped the first bombs. And as long as he has no good options for ending the conflict, he’s just going to keep lashing out at his domestic enemies like the governor of Minnesota.
news.summary: "Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota," said Trump.

news.title: 'Grossly Incompetent': Trump Blames Minnesota Officials, Not Iran, for Water System Cyberattacks
news.text: President Trump has pinned responsibility for cyberattacks on multiple water systems in Minnesota on state officials he has repeatedly clashed with, brushing aside reports suggesting Iranian hackers were behind the disruptions. The New York Times had reported that preliminary assessments from US and state officials pointed toward Iranian hackers as the likely culprits behind the attacks. Trump dismissed that conclusion during a cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday. He told those gathered that he had heard about the cyberattack in Minnesota and that officials there were blaming Iran, but said he did not buy it. Instead, he said he blamed Minnesota itself, calling the state grossly incompetent. "You know who's behind it? Minnesota - because they're grossly incompetent... I don't think there was an Iranian cyber attack. I think that Minnesota ought to get its act together," Trump said. "It's one of the worst-run states, JD (Vance) will tell you. He found tremendous corruption in Minnesota. And by the way, just gave me a report - MASSIVE future things having to do with corruption in Minnesota are happening right now," Trump added. A Long-Running Feud With Minnesota's GovernorTrump's comments fit into a broader pattern of tension between his administration and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat. Walz served as Kamala Harris' running mate during the 2024 presidential election, which Trump won alongside JD Vance. The relationship between Trump's administration and Minnesota authorities grew even more strained earlier this year after immigration agents killed two US citizens during street protests in the state. Trump elaborated further on his skepticism about Iran's involvement, saying the cyberattack hit 30 water treatment plants and that he placed the blame squarely on Minnesota and its governor, whom he described as corrupt. He argued that Iran would have to be lucky to pull off such an attack, suggesting the country has bigger problems to deal with than targeting Minnesota. “There was a cyber attack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, ‘Oh, it’s Iran.’ Iran should be so lucky. Iran’s got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota,” Trump said.

news.title: Jasmine Crockett Bashes Black Trump Supporters
news.text:
Soon-to-be former Democratic Rep. Jasmine Crockett (TX-30) has a huge problem with black people who don’t vote for her party.

During a recent panel discussion, Crockett recounted hearing from a young black woman who told her that her dad did not want to vote for former Vice President Kamala Harris. “He was like, ‘if I go vote, it’s going to be for Trump.’”

I don't want to ask.’ But nevertheless, One of the things that she said was, ‘my dad said he could trust Trump.’ And I was like, ‘really?’ And so the reality is that that's not the first time I've had that conversation,” Crockett continued.

Democrat Rep. I want those checks again,’ not understanding that really came from Congress,” and concluded that there is “an issue as it relates to civics in this country and people not understanding exactly how any of this works.” 

Crockett expressed similar sentiments in a December 2024 Vanity Fair interview where she said, “I will tell you that Black people historically have been fiercely loyal. That’s why you still see the [turnout] numbers that you see coming out for Black folks, even though there was a bit of flaking. In a February 2026 TMZ interview, the lawmaker bashed rapper Nicki Minaj for supporting Trump. “I just don’t do sellouts, especially in this moment,” she said, arguing that “Things are too serious. There are too many people that are being harmed.” 

She added, “And especially with her being an immigrant, then deciding to go and cozy up to this administration that is specifically putting targets on the backs of immigrants and anyone who stands with them … that is wrong, and I don’t even understand how you can play with it and pretend like it’s anything but wrong.”
