news.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Argument for America—and Against His Own Party
news.text:
Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen
Sign up for our daily newsletter to get the best of The New Yorker in your inbox.

El-Sayed is forty-one and the son of Egyptian immigrants. If elected, he would be the first Muslim ever to serve in the U.S. Senate. His opponent in the August 4th primary, Haley Stevens, represents the Party establishment: she has won endorsements from Governor Gretchen Whitmer and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. She is a former Obama Administration official who worked on the rescue of the car industry, which is an especially appealing credential in Michigan. Stevens and groups supporting her have spent sixty million dollars on ads—half of that sum has come from the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. At this point, polls suggest that El-Sayed is leading Stevens in the Democratic Party race, but in a general election he is trailing the Republican Mike Rogers by ten points, while Stevens is running even.
El-Sayed, who is both fluid and charming, also shows flashes of bravado and hauteur, particularly directed against his opponents. It was perhaps not a good idea, considering his Oxford and Ivy League bona fides, to say that Stevens could not “string together two coherent sentences.” According to Politico, El-Sayed recently said on a call with donors, referring to Senator John Fetterman, “You put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message, and all of a sudden starts to sound a lot different.” He is strong with younger voters; he is trailing with Black voters. He would ban ICE, withhold funding for arms for Israel, push for Medicare for All, and “get money out of politics.” Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
I want to start by going back to a formative moment, in 2007, when you were the commencement speaker for your class graduation at the University of Michigan. Bill Clinton addressed the class that day. He approached you afterward and told you that you were not only a terrific speaker but that you should consider a career in politics.
I’ll be honest with you—I literally laughed in his face. I mean, my name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. I got three names. Two of them, nobody knows how to pronounce. The first one is eleven letters long. To learn how to say it, you’ve got to realize that you got parts of your throat you didn’t know you had. People like me didn’t get to run for office. And that was 2007. So the first thing he asked me is, Why are you going to medical school? Which, when you’re a graduating senior who was the top student in your class, people don’t usually ask you that question, right? “Why are you doing that?”
In an accusatory way.
As if to sneer at your life choices. I was, like, Wait, what? I’m, like, Don’t you understand I’m brown and Muslim? It’s what we do. I was just grateful for the implicit compliment, but I was, like, I don’t get to run for office. And he thought about it for a minute, then he kind of chuckled and walked away.
Were you a Bill Clinton fan at that time?
I had really appreciated a lot of the global-health work that he had done. And obviously he was the President of my childhood. I was twenty-two years old in 2007. I had not seen Barack Obama. I mean, I watched him give the 2004 D.N.C. floor speech, but I hadn’t seen him on the national stage. That was still an untested hypothesis. And, also, as much as I enjoyed politics, I never saw myself as a participant. I wanted to be a doctor’s doctor. I thought I wanted to be a surgeon. I thought I wanted to take care of kids with spinal malformations, working in underserved places, and probably doing research in the area.
So you didn’t feel yourself to be a person of the left then? You weren’t critiquing Clinton—and eventually even Obama—as “neoliberal,” as the critique often goes from the left. You were looking at politics as something that you were interested in, only in a kind of more narrow way. Is that what you’re telling me?
I was, but not in the sense that there was anything I could do about it. I was more likely to be the kid you saw in the stacks at 11 P.M. than the kid you saw at the protest. We did some protesting when I was in college, but for me it was always, like: The way I want to change the world is as a doctor, and by getting health care to people who don’t have it. And, in some respects, in so many ways as a government official, and now running for office, a lot of folks want to paint me as, Oh, he wants to burn down the systems. No, I don’t. I want to bring my screwdriver and systematically deconstruct the parts of the system that are malforming and working for the wrong people. And I want to take the parts that have been misused there, and I want to rebuild that whole system so that it works for the people it needs to work for. I’m not a “burn it down” kind of personality. I’m a lot more of a: study it, understand how it works, think about how you could rebuild it—and then rebuild it.
Now, are you getting advice telling you that you need to say that, too? Because some people, I think it’s fair to say, in the press that I’ve read, Abdul, do see you as a “burn it down” kind of guy. And, running in the state of Michigan, maybe that’s not of universal appeal.
I’ll tell you this, David. The best single way to caricature me, as someone who has qualms with the system, is to try to flatten my personality into what they say they want me to be. And there are parts of me that say, Look, when I come with my tool kit to try and deconstruct it, and you want to stop me from doing it and you get in my way, we’re going to have words. I’m not afraid of a fight. But I also am not the kind of person who’s just coming to destroy anything. I’m coming to build things that people need and deserve.
Obviously the narrative is what it is. When you get sixty million dollars spent against you, they’re going to “burn it to the ground.” I mean, they’ve tried to construct all kinds of narratives about me—as a function of my personality, as a function of my background, and as a set of tropes that are easily told about somebody like me. But the thing I have learned, after having run for office twice now, is that there’s going to be a narrative built around you. And the best thing that you can do is just to show up and be who you are.
You mentioned the Obama ascension, the Obama [convention] speech in 2004, and then his Presidency from 2008 onward. How do you look at that Presidency? What was constructive about it, and what’s your critique of it?
I don’t get to do what I’m doing without President Obama doing what he did. The parallels are kind of uncanny. And I remember watching that 2004 speech and just being, like, I didn’t know politics could look like that or sound like that. His dad emigrated from Africa. My dad emigrated from a different part of Africa. He had mixed parents. I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, Jackie, who’s a Daughter of the American Revolution. I mean, he had a funny name; I’ve got a funny name. The one place it doesn’t work is he’s tall and skinny, and I’m pretty short and thick. But I don’t get to do what I do without him.
At the same time, when you love somebody like that, you’re going to look at them and say, Could we do more? It’s kind of like the way you think about your parents. You know what I mean? You love and revere your parents, and you’re grateful for all they did to help you. And, look, my dad was a child of an illiterate homemaker who was the smartest person I ever met in my life, who lost two of her infant children. And his father, who had an eighth-grade education, sold vegetables in a fish market. My dad studied my life into existence. I’m so grateful for him. And, at the same time, anybody who watches their parents will always look and say, Hey, if I don’t build off of what I saw, then what am I even doing here? I kind of think about President Obama the same way.
I was in medical school during the Affordable Care Act fights. And the big frustration I had is, like, why are we not going all the way? Why are we accommodating the private-health-insurance industry? And that, to me, was a righteous kind of frustration. And, at the same time, I have had my career in the world of the A.C.A., and I can’t imagine just how much worse it would be had we not gotten that. So you can both say the A.C.A. was incredible, and, as the President said, this was a starter home. I think it’s about damn time we move out of the starter home. We’ve outgrown it.
I spent some time with Obama, in writing about him, and I had a very interesting experience with him once. I was asking him about race—we were in the Oval Office talking about that. And he was very hesitant to answer the questions I was asking him. I even asked him about Malcolm X. And it’s not that he got up and ran out of the room, but—he’s a gifted politician, and he knows how to not answer something while answering it. And then he left the Oval Office, was three-quarters of the way down the hall, and then came all the way back and said to me, “You know, no matter what I say about these things, it has an incredibly volcanic effect on the public, as President. No matter what.” Temperamentally, you can see he’s a very deliberative, careful guy. What about that do you admire, and what about that do you depart from?
I ran for governor in 2018. I was thirty-three; I’d never run for office in my life. And I learned what it was like to be in the public eye to that level. And it is a very difficult thing, because you’re not necessarily offered your full humanity, because you’re constantly speaking in the context of a set of narrative efforts to try to frame what you say against you. You can say three sentences, but they’ll pick one sentence out of context to frame you in the narrative that they choose to frame you in.
Can you give me an example?
If I speak at all about righteous anger, then I’m an Arab guy speaking about anger. If I criticize my male Republican opponent and also criticize my female Democratic opponent, then the only thing that is talked about is my criticism of my female Democratic opponent, specifically around her gender. And it’s just the nature of what this system is, and how our politics are transacted in sound bites. So I empathize entirely. And I’ll tell you, this time around, I do think that we’re operating in a very different moment than he was operating in, because of the ubiquity of social media. So I can move a lot more of myself, and the full dynamism of myself, to tell my whole story. This time, when I decided to run, there was still always this question of, like: How mad on behalf of other people can I be?
I’m pretty damn pissed off on behalf of other people. I went to medical school because I wanted to be a doctor only to realize that our health-care system was actively—actively!—pushing out the people I wanted to take care of. And I’ll be honest with you: Very few people say they got radicalized in med school. But when I watched our health-care system, on the ninth floor of the extremely prestigious hospital that I was training in, we had people playing pianos for foreign dignitaries coming to get heart procedures. Then, in the basement, watching indigent New Yorkers get, in effect, pushed out of the health-care system before they got the care they needed—it really changed the way I thought about our system. And that’s the side of things that I’ve had to struggle with. How righteously mad can I be on behalf of people who’ve had a system that is architected against them in ways that actively lie to them? That shit pisses me off!
Is there, in the global picture of things, a health-care system that you look at that you’d like to transplant into the United States?
There are parts of different health-care systems I’d like to. And here’s the thing about it: Look, my life is an accident of history. I know what my life would have been, but for the accident that I was born in America. And, my grandmother, when I’d go to Egypt, she would do everything that she could to hammer that in. To be, like, The only thing you’ve got over any of your cousins, who are just as smart, just as anything as you, is that you get to go back to America at the end of the summer.
And the thing about America is that we don’t do things like other people. We do them better. I mean, I love that about our country. And, it’s funny, when we talk about health care, there’s always this sense of, like, Well, whose health-care system do you want then? I’m, like, I don’t know. I want an American health-care system that’s just better! I think we could do a single-payer system better than any country in the world. Do you know why? We already spend nineteen per cent of our whole G.D.P. on health care.
I’m just, like: Why do we ever limit ourselves on anything? We are the richest, most powerful, most innovative country in the history of the world. And you want to tell me that the best we can do is charge people so much effing money that we owe two hundred and twenty-five billion dollars of medical debt as a country? That’s the best we can do? Come on, y’all, this is America! I’ve seen what America can do for people. I also see too often what America does not do for too many of her kids. And that’s why I’m doing this.
We’re right now looking at a health-care system that’s not only characterized by all the faults that you’re describing but also the specifics of having R.F.K., Jr., and the MAHA movement as the most prominent voices in the health sphere. How do we go about rebuilding trust in public health?
Let me tell you a story, David, because I think it helps to explain this. During the height of the pandemic, I was talking to a group—outdoors, fully masked, et cetera—about taking the vaccine. And I’m never going to forget this gentleman. I had been the health commissioner for the city of Detroit, talking about getting this vaccine, how critical it was. He said, “Look, man, I know you. I’ve seen you”—I was on CNN at the time—“I trust you. I’m going to get my vaccine, but it’s just weird to me that you all are out here, trying to get me to take a vaccine that didn’t exist a year ago, for a disease that didn’t exist a year ago, when I can’t afford my insulin, which is a medication that’s existed for, like, a hundred years, and is for a disease I have had my whole life. When are you all going to show up to make sure I get to take my insulin?” And I was, like, Damn—you’re right.
I’m not quite clear what you’re saying. You’re saying, Abdul, that the mistrust was such that it opened the door to conspiracy thinking?
Exactly. It’s that, once you don’t trust the industry, because it’s so expensive, and they’re so clearly trying to pick your pocket—at that point, it’s not that hard for somebody like an R.F.K., Jr., to come in here and then say, “Well, you don’t even need the things that they make anyway. Here are these alternatives that they’re keeping you from. They don’t want you to know!” And I think, to build trust again, we have to address the greed part in the system. Because, once people feel like they can get access to the things that science has delivered, I think it becomes a lot easier, then, to have an honest conversation about: What is the best way to prevent measles? What is the best way to protect ourselves from cyclosporiasis? But we live in a moment right now, in Michigan, which is crazy to me, where we’re dodging lettuce.
And we just had the worst air quality of our history, for the second summer in a row. I mean, air quality and lettuce were the two things that I tried to dodge in my summers in Egypt. And so I think we’re at a moment right now where we’re seeing the end outcome of disinvesting in public health. And I think we have an opportunity—if we’re serious about taking on the corporations that have been monetizing our health-care system and killing trust—to actually be able to rebuild trust again.
Now, a freshman senator—they can vote on everything, but in order to make real headway, they usually come down to one issue. Would you say that health care is going to be yours?
Health care and the thing that’s keeping us from having health care, which is money in politics.
Tell me what your first steps are.
So, God willing, we take the majority. We’re in the Senate. I’ve got two jobs from that point on. And I also want to remember that politics is path-dependent. There’s a story that’s constantly being told. And the fact that you and I are having this conversation is a function of the fact that this is not just any Senate race. AIPAC and all the powers that be have effed around, and made this the highest-stakes Senate race, probably this cycle and for a long time. And when you spend sixty million dollars to beat one person and they beat you, you just turned that person into David. You gave me a gigantic platform. Thank you so much, AIPAC donors. I’m so grateful for you. And that means that I have an opportunity here to use that platform to move a set of conversations.
I’ve got two jobs when I get to the U.S. Senate. No. 1, throw as much sand in the gears of the Trump Administration as possible. If I get a seat on that HELP committee [the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions], which I hope I will, then it’s the opportunity to haul up a guy like R.F.K., Jr., and start asking and start connecting dots to how much money he’s actually made on the grift, and people around him have made on the grift. It’s hauling up Big Pharma and talking about how much money they’ve made on their grift.
You’re accusing R.F.K. of making money on the grift. What do you mean?
That reporting is out there, around his many connections to folks who have profiteered off of an anti-vaccine movement. And then, for Big Pharma—I mean, this is an obvious grift. They just are able to buy off politicians on both sides of the aisle to make sure that they can continue to have very little pushback when they want to raise prescription-drug prices. So I want to call that out, because they’re connected.
And then the other thing I’ve got to do in those first two years is use the incredible platform that AIPAC and all these mega-donors are giving me, to move the conversation about who we are and who we want to be, to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for All, and lay the groundwork, through the state of Michigan, for a President who is going to act on Day One to do these things.
Abdul, your name has been connected quite often with the kind of left-leaning energy in the Party—Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Bernie Sanders, Zohran Mamdani. And yet you have not joined the Democratic Socialists—the D.S.A. Why not?
Too much of a scientist, I guess. I’m a capitalist who reads about capitalism. And when you read about capitalism, it is very clear, even to the originators who coined the idea, that the biggest risk to capitalism was not going to be government regulation, as much as the corporatists want you to think it is. It was always going to be monopoly. And we know that hyper-capitalism tends toward monopoly. We also understand that that happens in part because, when a corporation gets big enough, it has enough power to start “rent seeking,” which is a fancy way of saying influencing government action to protect its own interests. And that’s the place we are right now in capitalism. I think small business is amazing. I think it’s a really efficient way to move capital into the areas where it can be really efficient to create a lot of jobs. I’m just not a socialist. And so I want capitalism to work the way it was supposed to work, not the way that the corporations tell us it’s supposed to work.
Abdul, forgive me. I’m sure people in Michigan know the answer to this—but the presumptive Republican candidate in the race, Mike Rogers, recently told supporters, in a private call, that if you win the nomination, he is “in good shape.”
Man hasn’t been in good shape since the nineties, but, yeah.
Well, this was reported by CNN, I think. What’s your reaction to that? Why do you think he says it, and why do you think he might be wrong?
I think he says it because all of his base understands the risk of actually having to go up against somebody who’s willing to take the fight to them. And here’s why he’s wrong: In the nineties, you asked for tens of millions of dollars from your benefactors. Then you put thirty-second ads on TV, and then you won because you were able to get more money and spend more on TV. What I’m proving is that you can win a race without that. I mean, we’re being outspent, what, twelve to one, right now? AIPAC, Big Pharma, Big Tech, Blue Cross Blue Shield, [the Detroit-based energy company] D.T.E., our local utility—all of them bearing down. They’re so mad that we’re still up. And we’re going to win. And I think what we’re showing is that if you can move your message, and it is consistent and authentic to who you are, people see past the thirty-second ads on TV—because, guess what? Nobody likes the commercial part of a TV show. Nobody’s ever, like, Man, I can’t wait to watch the commercials.
So all that is to say that he’s just got an old-fashioned view of politics. And this is why, in fact, it’s that old-fashioned view of politics, which is itself so hypocritical and damning. It’s the idea that you got to cozy up to the people with all the money who can then buy you all the ads that help you win. And it’s the fact that he’s cozying up to all the money, which, in effect, I’m going to wrap around him over and over and over again. This is a guy who took six figures from the pharmaceutical industry; voted, I don’t know how many times, to raise prescription-drug prices; helped to architect the opioid epidemic! And then made fourteen million dollars after his time [in Congress] from Florida, where he moved into a McMansion. I mean, the guy would rather be golfing in Florida. And even there, he’s, like, the beta character in the show. He’s the one who laughs extra loud. He’s just confused about who he is. He wants to be ultra-MAGA, but he was very against Donald Trump, which is why his own base is kind of circumspect about him. I’m, like, Bro, you can’t serve three masters. The people, Donald Trump, and then your golf buddies: which one are you going to actually serve? I’m going to force him into conniptions, and it’s going to be a lot of fun.
Abdul, for the sake of clarity, because we get this kind of information in bits and pieces in the way of the information universe here—I totally understand your outrage about the Gaza war. I totally understand your critique of October 7th. It’s not like you endorsed October 7th, as unfortunately some people have. But it seems that you get very prickly when you’re asked the question: Does Israel have a right to exist? You come from a country that, in the late seventies, made its accommodation, a kind of rough peace, between Egypt and Israel, under Anwar Sadat, as did Jordan, eventually. And God knows there are still problems in the region between and among those countries. But what is your hope for a resolution in the Middle East? Is it two states? Is it one state? What underlies your sense of the situation there?
Well, David, since you’re giving me some time for nuance—I deeply appreciate it—allow me some nuance.

No. 1, I think we often frame the conversation around what’s happening there rather than what’s happening here. What’s happening here is that there are communities where the median income is fourteen thousand dollars a year. And those kids go without good schools and those kids go without functional infrastructure.
I think the foundational question to me is: What do we owe those kids around their tax dollars? No. 1. No. 2, I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination, for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike. And I believe that it is not my job as an American policymaker to decide what the ultimate peace should be. But it is my job to make sure that our resources are stewarded correctly for the people I’m responsible for: those kids going to those broken schools.
I also believe that it is my job to do that doubly when we exist in a kind of hypocrisy around how we’ve thought about that issue for a very long time. The very same people who tell you you have to believe in a two-state solution are constantly aiding, arming, and abetting an Israeli government that has been dead set on foreclosing on the possibility of a Palestinian state since we’ve been funding them. So forgive me if I’m not going to play the cosplay thing, where I allow the money that should be spent taking care of our kids to be sent to a military that has done a genocide—at baseline, does apartheid, and is now attempting the annexation of southern Lebanon—to foreclose on the possibility of Palestinian self-determination.
So here’s what I believe. I believe we have a responsibility to uphold international law. I believe we have a responsibility to treat every single state the same way, around international law. I believe in a process that offers a free Palestinian people the equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination that a free Jewish Israeli people ought to have. And then I will support whatever the outcome is that a free Palestinian people and a free Jewish Israeli people decide is the right outcome. If that’s two states, great, I’m for it. If it’s one state, I’m for that. If it’s this “land for all” model, or twenty-three states, or whatever it is that they decide. But I am not O.K. saying that, as a senator from Michigan, I’m going to take tax dollars from Michigan, send them to a foreign government that does heinous things in contraposition to the ideals that I support, and then sit here and be, like, Yes, but I’m for a two-state solution—when I know that the current status quo is never ever going to allow that to happen.
You campaigned with Hasan Piker. And I don’t think anybody would say that you have to be in complete accord with anybody that either supports you or votes for you or campaigns for you—but that was a prominent thing. It was in the national press. And he has said things like he “doesn’t have an issue with Hezbollah.” That was a quote. He said that Mao Zedong was a great leader. How much do you depart from Hasan Piker? Where do you accept his support, and where do you get down in the trenches with him and argue?
I mean, he and I are not going to agree on everything. And we’ve debated this. He has some positions—
Do you find those statements repellent?
Yeah, I disagree with him. But here’s the thing, right? On the same day that I campaigned with Hasan, I went on “Fox & Friends.” I find a lot of the things that the people on “Fox & Friends” say repellent. The fact that they platform Donald Trump. The fact that Donald Trump himself had dinner with Nick Fuentes—
Wait. I don’t think anybody has any illusions that your next job is going to be as a cast member on Fox.
Fox is basically W.W.E., verbally, for old folk. And, if I’m the face, you could imagine I just go on there and just get the steel chair in my head every day. Not going to be my next job—because I’ll be in the U.S. Senate.
The point that I’m making here is that I think there is this failure that we have in understanding what democracy is for in the first place. Democracy is the technology by which we solve our differences peaceably. And, in going and talking to different groups of people, what I’m trying to do is create a pathway for people into the democratic process by offering them a perspective that they might agree with. And I think there’s this platform politics that we’ve had since the twenty-twenties. And I thought we rejected it—because, let’s not forget, Hasan was invited to stream from the D.N.C. by Vice-President [Kamala] Harris in 2024. Let’s not forget that.
But, in campaigning with him, everybody was, like, Well, how could you possibly? And I was, like, Did we not learn our lesson that we need to go talk to people who have large audiences, who have felt locked out of the political process for a very long time? And even though he and I might have differences—there are things I disagree with him on—he has an audience of nearly three million people who watch him regularly. And I really want to show that audience that there is a way forward, where you can stand up for a politics that’s more about guaranteeing you health care than sending bombs to drop on other people, that is willing to stand forthrightly against genocide wherever you see it. And though he and I might disagree on China or cars, and certainly he said some things that I find deeply distasteful, that does not mean that I should not go and speak to his audience and speak to him. And I think the faster Democrats recognize that, the faster we’re going to be on a pathway to actually winning elections.
One of the illusions that Trump held out is that he would bring manufacturing back to big manufacturing states. And anybody who knows anything about Michigan—and not just Detroit but across the state—knows that it has suffered terribly from deindustrialization over time. Is he selling snake oil there? Is that something to bring back? Is that a desirable thing? How do jobs come back to a Midwestern state like Michigan?
I think it is possible. I think it is not possible the way he’s done it. The through line for Donald Trump is, Donald Trump will do whatever gives him attention and adoration in the moment. That’s kind of what he is. And he wants money, which gives him attention and adoration. That’s the Donald Trump trick. He is a pathological narcissist who is, like, the endgame of narcissism—and he’s very, very charming. He’s very, very good at telling you what you want to hear. When he came in, he was not a part of the political system, and people give him a lot of credit for that. Ask yourself: How much must people hate the political system if they were willing to give their vote to a narcissistic, megalomaniac billionaire? People gave him the benefit of the doubt because they hated the system worse.
So, I think you can actually build manufacturing jobs again, but not this way. If you were to do it, here’s how you do it. No. 1, you would need to invest massively in research and development for high-manufacturing-potential industries. To me, that is, yes, auto, but it’s auto in the place that auto is going—both maintaining our lead when it comes to internal-combustion engines, but also the future of E.V.s, which have overtaken markets all over the rest of the world. It’s also green technology and the ability to create renewable energy quickly. And then what you would do is invest in early-stage startups and legacy corporations in ways that were targeted on jobs and jobs and jobs, not targeted on stock buybacks and stock performance. And then you would create very specific tariffs that were extremely transparent, specifically around protecting those growing industries. And then you would subsidize those industries in a big way. If we want to actually win the future of auto, we need to continue to be the best at building internal-combustion engines.
I would also love to see us subsidize E.V. manufacturing so that you can get a twenty-five-thousand-dollar, three-hundred-mile-range car, anywhere and everywhere. And we have the charging-station infrastructure to do it. If we were willing to do that for ten years—not these seventy-five-hundred-dollar tax credits for cars that only rich people can afford. I’m talking about a twenty-five-thousand-dollar, three-hundred-mile range E.V. That’s the metric. And we’ll get it to twenty-five thousand dollars. If we did that, we would immediately become the world’s leader in E.V.s. Why? Because we have the best manufacturing technology, best manufacturing talent, and best engineering talent in the world. We’re just not investing in them. And, too often, the Big Three have been more interested in the quarterly bottom line and stock buybacks than they have been in the next ten years of their industry, which is why we see this schizophrenic approach to whether or not we are going to, or are not going to, make E.V.s.
How do you feel about artificial intelligence and its potential as an economic driver and its effect on the job market?
I’m worried as hell. And I’m worried as hell because this is the first technology that young people are rejecting outright. I see the risk on three different fronts. The first one is in the built environment. You’ve got this data-center explosion that is being done in ways that are not protecting people from the real risks. The second is the existential risk of A.I. itself. I mean, we just had, last week, an OpenAI model that slipped its human-design sandbox and went and did a cyberattack on a website. And then the third is the way that A.I. can foundationally change the social contract. And I think we need leadership and we need leadership now. And here’s the danger: there are two warring A.I. super PACs out there—each a nine-figure super PAC—and they’re trying to make it ungovernable. So, if we don’t have leaders who both understand the tech and are not bought off by the tech, I’m worried about where we go.
Well, in the medical field—and I speak to you as somebody of real knowledge—A.I. is potentially going to be an incredible boon, both to medical research and medical practice.
It could. And, look, I think that’s great. The problem right now is that that’s not the incentive that they’re driving. They keep telling us this, but then I keep hearing headlines about how many jobs are lost. And here’s the other side of it: toward what incentive? The technology, David—I’m not against the technology. I think the technology’s incredible. I’m against the incentives driving the technology. And I think we need to rethink those incentives.
Now, many Democrats would like to distance themselves from identity politics, trans rights, saying that so-called kitchen-table issues are the prime issues, and that any emphasis on identity drives people away. You’ve heard this a lot from Rahm Emanuel; you’ve heard it from Gavin Newsom. How do you respond to that impulse?
The idea that we can assent to the taking away of anybody’s rights, and think that somehow the government won’t come for all of our rights, is itself the problem. And, look, I don’t need people to understand how they use their rights. I just need people to agree that the government shouldn’t be able to take any of our rights. I put my face on the ground thirty-four times a day, David. Most people don’t understand why I do it. I don’t need them to understand. I just want to have the right to do it. And when people decide that they want to take away my right to do that, I’ve got a problem.
Now, I hope that everybody’s going to show up and say, No, no, no. You can’t stop that person or that community from reflecting and praying as they choose. Similarly, when it comes to trans rights, this is the right to get the health care that you need. That’s really what it comes down to. It’s the right to be who you are. It’s the right not to be discriminated against by your government because of who you are. Because what tends to happen is they come for theirs, then they come for yours, then they come for theirs. And at some point you live in a society where rights are negotiable, and that is not the America I was born in. It’s not the America I know and love. It’s not the America I’m going to allow somebody like Donald Trump to give us.
Finally: Let’s assume, for a moment, that the Democrats take the House and maybe even take the Senate—although that’s a far more difficult proposition. How does that change the course of politics for the next two years?
It sets us on a pathway to being able to hold Donald Trump accountable, and actually reflect the rule of law, because we’ve enforced it. It sets us on a pathway toward electing a President who actually wants to govern with purpose, rather than just not be Donald Trump. People are not asking this question of, like, Where am I on a left-right spectrum? What’s the future of the Democratic Party? They’re asking, Am I going to be able to afford getting health care if I get sick? Am I going to be able to pay next month’s mortgage? What the hell—I can’t actually fill up my tank of gas. Who’s going to do something about that?
That has to be the be-all and end-all of our politics. Everything else starts from there. So we’ve got to stop compromising when it comes to the corporations who are making people’s lives harder. We’ve got to stop compromising when it comes to anybody’s rights. We’ve got to stop compromising on the idea that ICE is bad and immigration is good. These are not hard arguments to make in America. Have some courage and go make them. ♦
news.summary: The Michigan U.S. Senate candidate on campaigning with Hasan Piker, being a capitalist, and why his fellow-Democrats need to “stop compromising.”

news.title: '60 Minutes' Civil War: 'Two Camps' Spark Internal Chaos at Crisis-Hit Show as 'New Guard' Takes Over, Insiders Claim
news.text:
Civil war has broken out at 60 Minutes after the troubled CBS News show fractured into two rival camps, according to new claims.

RadarOnline.com can reveal the long-running news magazine faces an uncertain future due to the infighting.'It's Old School Versus New School'Since new boss Bari Weiss overhauled the show along with freshly-appointed exec producer Nick Bilton, insiders claim staffers have split into new rival camps.

Taking to his Naughty But Nice Substack page, a source claimed to Rob Shuter: "It's old school versus new school, and they barely acknowledge each other anymore.

"Every editorial meeting feels like a fight over what 60 Minutes should be. The tension is thick enough to cut with a knife."

According to insiders, the younger journalists brought in to modernize the broadcast believe the show’s legendary formula no longer fits today's media landscape.Lesley Stahl Nicknamed 'Grandma' By NewcomersA separate CBS insider claimed: "They think the legacy team is stuck in another era. Behind closed doors, some have even started calling Lesley Stahl 'Grandma.'

"It's incredibly disrespectful, but it shows just how deep the generational divide has become."

Veteran staffers, meanwhile, believe the newcomers are disrespecting the type of journalism that made 60 Minutes one of television’s most respected institutions.

An insider said: "The old guard believes they're protecting the soul of the show The new crowd thinks they’re tearing down a museum and building something audiences will actually watch."'The New Guard Was Hired To Take Control'Another source said: "The new guard was hired to take control. This isn’t a transition — it's a takeover. The people trying to preserve the past are running out of allies."

Former 60 Minutes chief Bill Owens is reportedly planning a scathing tell-all memoir that will call out CBS News and Paramount one year after he resigned from the popular news program.

However, this has sparked concerns, as Owens is still believed to be receiving a hefty multimillion-dollar payout as part of his separation agreement.

In the tell-all, he's set to discuss President Trump's lawsuit over the editing of former Vice President Kamala Harris' 60 Minutes interview during the 2024 election, as well as the subsequent settlement, which Owens described as "perhaps the worst legal strategy ever employed by the worst-run media company in the history of America," per Breaker Media.He also reportedly suggested that senior management was placing political affiliation before journalism.

Owens' separation agreement with the company reportedly included a non-disparagement clause, which could potentially be broken depending on the content of his upcoming book, according to the New York Post and Puck News. 

However, no lawsuits have been filed as of yet, according to the outlets.

Last year, Owens resigned after more than 30 years at CBS News, several months before new network boss Weiss took over. 

"Over the past months, it has … become clear that I would not be allowed to run the show as I have always run it, to make independent decisions based on what was right for 60 Minutes, right for the audience," Owens told staff in an April 2025 memo, according to NBC News.

"So, having defended this show – and what we stand for – from every angle, over time with everything I could, I am stepping aside so the show can move forward," he added.
news.summary: Civil war has broken out at '60 Minutes' after the troubled CBS News show fractured into two rival camps since Bari Weiss's overhaul, according to new claims.

news.title: New York sues Kalshi, says its prediction markets are ‘illegal gambling’
news.text:
New York officials have sued prediction market platform Kalshi, calling it an “illegal, unlicensed gambling operation” as the state seeks to halt its operations and force the company to forfeit its profits.

With its lawsuit on Friday, New York joins a growing number of states filing cases against Kalshi and other companies in a dispute with United States President Donald Trump’s administration over who regulates the fast-growing prediction market. Kalshi and other platforms argue they are federally licensed and regulated, and states have no authority to govern them.

In a petition filed in a state court in Manhattan, Attorney General Letitia James said Kalshi failed to obtain a New York State Gaming Commission licence to operate its platform, where people trade based on the predicted outcomes of sport, elections and other events.

The attorney general said such platforms can encourage problem gambling, including by people under age 21, and endanger people’s financial, emotional and physical health.

James’s office is requesting that Kalshi be ordered to forfeit all illegal gains, pay restitution to consumers who were harmed and pay fines equal to three times the company’s gains.

Kalshi had been in negotiations with New York officials in recent weeks over tax and consumer protection issues.

James filed similar petitions in April against two other prediction market operators – Coinbase Financial Markets and Gemini Titan – saying all three companies’ so-called event contracts were “quintessentially” gambling.

“New York’s gambling laws protect children from underage betting and help combat gambling addiction,” James said in a statement. “No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple.”

CFTC challenges

Prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket have soared in popularity since the 2024 US presidential election, when they fared better than pollsters in predicting Republican Donald Trump’s victory over Democrat Kamala Harris.

The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has claimed exclusive jurisdiction to regulate transactions offered in the prediction market and challenged regulatory activity in at least nine states, including New York, which it sued in April.

States counter that the vast majority of the business on prediction market platforms is sport betting, which they are empowered to regulate, and that is completely different from the commodities and futures contracts that the commission regulates.

CFTC filed an “emergency” motion in the federal court late on Thursday night to stop New York from subjecting Kalshi to state gambling laws, calling it “overreach” that would irreparably harm the agency and markets it regulates.

Kalshi is based in New York. The company expected James’s lawsuit, calling it “political theater from the leadership in our own state,” and sought to move it to Manhattan federal court eight hours after the attorney general filed it.

New York “seeks to place itself in the position of a nationwide derivatives regulator,” Kalshi said. “Through this action — which seeks to shut Kalshi down nationwide — New York seeks to fundamentally subvert the exclusive jurisdiction of the CFTC.”

On Wednesday, the federal appeals court in Manhattan rejected Kalshi’s request to avoid possible enforcement activity, while it appeals US District Judge Analisa Torres’s refusal on July 8 to issue an injunction against the state. Kalshi pre-emptively sued New York last October to block such activity.

Prediction market wagers

According to New York’s petition, Kalshi’s prediction markets are gambling because people can wager on events whose outcomes they don’t control, such as who will win the Super Bowl or the reality TV show “Big Brother”.

New York also objected to Kalshi letting 18- to 20-year-olds use its platform, despite a minimum age of 21 under state law for mobile sport betting.

“Kalshi has chosen to ignore New York’s gaming laws, which exist to protect consumers, prevent problematic gambling, deliver funding for critical public services, and ensure that every company plays by the same rules,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement. “This choice has consequences.”

At least four states — Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada and Washington — have won court orders restricting Kalshi’s activities.

In refusing to stop potential New York enforcement activity, Torres found the state’s interests in preventing gambling addiction, preserving the integrity of sport, and avoiding a proliferation of unregulated contracts “heavily” outweighed Kalshi’s interests in ensuring the primacy of federal law and avoiding “intractable” technology issues for customers.

On Monday, a federal judge temporarily blocked Minnesota’s first-in-the-nation law banning prediction markets just days before it was to take effect — dealing a setback for states trying to outlaw or regulate the platforms.
news.summary: New York is one of many states with cases against Kalshi and others in dispute with Trump gov't on who gets to regulate.

news.title: Brittney Griner files for divorce from wife of 7 years who fought for her release from Russia
news.text: WNBA player Brittney Griner has filed for divorce from her wife of seven years, Cherelle, court records show. Cherelle was a vocal voice during Griner's Russian imprisonment, constantly pleading with U.S. government officials to bring the former Atlanta Dream star home. When Griner returned home in late 2022, she thanked then-President Joe Biden for his efforts. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM "Over the last 9 months you have been so privy to one of the darkest moments of my life and so today I’m just standing here overwhelmed with emotions but the most important emotion that I have right now is just sincere gratitude for President Biden and his entire administration," Cherelle said with Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris by her side. Cherelle thanked several members of the Biden administration, Griner's former Phoenix Mercury, the WNBPA and Brittney’s agency for doing all they could to keep the WNBA superstar in the spotlight after she was detained, sentenced and then transferred to a Russian penal colony in the final moments of her detention. "Today, my family is whole. But as you all are aware," Cherelle added. "There are so many other families who are not whole. BG’s not here to say this, but I will gladly speak on her behalf and say that BG and I will remain committed to the work on getting every American home, including Paul (Whelan) whose family is in our hearts today as we celebrate BG being home. We do understand that there’s still people out here who are enduring what I endured the last 9 months of missing, tremendously, their loved ones." The Griners married in 2019 and share a son, but the WNBA star, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, said the marriage was "irretrievably broken." WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT Griner was freed in a prisoner exchange for convicted Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout. She was arrested at Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow on Feb. 17, 2022, after Russian authorities said she had vape cartridges with cannabis oil inside her luggage. On Aug. 4 of that year, Griner was given a nine-year sentence after pleading guilty, arguing that she had been prescribed cannabis for her pain and inadvertently packed it. Her sentence was upheld in October, and she was later transferred to a penal colony. Bout is known as the "Merchant of Death" and the possible swap for him was floated back in May. He was in the middle of a 25-year sentence in federal prison after he was convicted of conspiracy to kill Americans relating to the support of a Colombian terrorist organization. Griner wrote in her memoir that she expected Cherelle to get a divorce if she had actually stayed in Russia for her entire prison sentence. "My basketball career would be over. I’d be in my early forties and out of shape, would have to find a new way to provide for my wife. And Relle. She assured me she’d wait, but ten years was ridiculous," Griner wrote, via Complex. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a billionaire Trump supporter, said the Ceuta situation was caused by Spain's policy of offering hundreds of thousands of migrants already in the country a legal status.

news.title: Chicago Socialists Meetings to Discuss New Party and 2028 Presidential Candidate
news.text:
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), who have defeated several Democrat incumbents this election cycle, will be hosting their “Socialists Summit” this weekend, July 31-August 2, in Chicago. At this summit, the DSA will offer socialist organizing training to its participants, including on “Governing as Socialists” and on “Building to a General Strike.” This event will include a surprise keynote speaker, and all those who attend will have to submit a negative COVID test.

At the same time, the Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA), “the youth and student section of the Democratic Socialists of America,” are holding their convention, where they will be voting on whether to field and endorse a presidential candidate in 2028, as well as on whether to call for a new party outside the Democratic Party.

The YDSA will be voting on several resolutions at the convention, most of them having to do with forming and supporting labor movements and other Socialist organizations. One of the more noteworthy resolutions is resolution 18, titled “Preparing for a Class-Struggle 2028 Presidential election.” If adopted, the YDSA would move to create an infrastructure to support a potential DSA candidate for president.

In one of the resolution’s preambles, the YDSA criticize Kamala Harris for being too rightwing. In another, it characterizes the Democratic Party as “class-collaborationist,” and states its aim to “build an independent, socialist political force fighting to win a majority of society over to our politics,” implying that it believes a Democratic Socialist could win a majority of Americans over to the movement, despite the party’s many radical proposals. 

If DSA were to advance a presidential candidate, the YDSA would not “hide, minimize, or alter [their] platform and vision” for the sake of appealing to more voters. It also promises to criticize and differentiate itself from the DSA candidate, if it deems necessary, a strategy quite uncommon in presidential elections.

The young Democratic Socialists will also be voting on a resolution (23) to call for the creation a new Socialist party in America:

“Let it be resolved that the signatories of this resolution motion for the creation of a Socialist Party independent of the Democratic Party; one which should be fit for competing in state & local races no later than 2028, a roadmap to the accomplishment of which DSA/YDSA invites, as equals, other anti-capitalist, anti-imperialist & anti-Zionist associations or parties to participate in drafting.”

According to the resolution, the DSA would invite other current leftwing organizations, including the Working Families Party, the Communist Party USA, and the Green Party into a new party, a “Socialist Party.” The resolution does not explicitly rule out contesting Democrat primaries, as the DSA has been winning many of them. It does, however, signal opposition to working within the Democratic Party framework, and accuses the Democrats of favoring “Fascists” to Socialists, while indicating a belief that Socialist candidates could win apart from the Democratic Party:

“Whereas the recent successes of openly socialist candidates (DSA or otherwise) in state & local elections have demonstrated clearly the political appetite for a Socialist Party independent of the Democratic Party.”…“Whereas the liberal capitalists in control of the Democratic Party would sooner do battle with socialists than with fascists.”

The Democratic Socialists of America currently have negative net favorability. According to a July 15th Echelon insights poll, 25% of Americans have a very or somewhat favorable view of the DSA, while 46% have a very or somewhat unfavorable view. A CNN poll suggests that around one in three Democrats identify as Democratic Socialists, though it is unclear whether they would leave the Democratic Party to vote for hypothetical Socialist Party candidates.

news.title: Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has thoughts about toning down political fights. Here's what he says
news.text:
OKLAHOMA CITY (AP) — The last time Gov. Kevin Stitt of Oklahoma hosted the nation’s governors, it didn’t go so well.

The annual gathering of state leaders in Washington in February was overshadowed by a fight with President Donald Trump, who refused to allow two governors — both Democrats — to attend a White House meeting. As head of the National Governors Association, Stitt successfully pressed Trump to reverse course but got an earful in the process.

Trump, who carried each of Oklahoma’s 77 counties in 2024, blasted Stitt as a “RINO,” meaning Republican in name only, and criticized the term-limited governor’s performance in office.

Stitt is again hosting his colleagues this weekend, this time on his home turf in Oklahoma City as he turns over leadership of the National Governors Association to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat and one of the governors Trump had sought to exclude. In an interview, Stitt discussed the dust-up with Trump, warned against efforts to federalize elections, and expressed concern that a mammoth federal government has contributed to the country’s tense political climate.

Here are highlights of the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

THE ASSOCIATED PRESS: You’ve spent the past year working closely with governors from both parties. What have you learned?

STITT: We agree on much more than we disagree. I was never in politics until I ran for governor. I’m like everybody else. I’m watching Fox News. I’m in my camp, and the other guys are in the MSNBC camp, and we’re over here thinking the other people are bad. But when I get in these roles and I meet the governor of Maryland and the governor of New York and these other governors, I realize that, literally, we’re all Americans.

AP: You’ve talked a lot about states’ rights. Going into the midterms, are you confident that states will be able to conduct their elections without interference from Trump or the federal government?

STITT: You know, I do.

First off, I don’t think that we should federalize the elections at all. I believe that is a state issue. The states should control their own elections. Should we make sure they’re done fairly and U.S. citizens are voting? 100%. I think there’s broad agreement with that. Oklahoma, literally, all of our absentee ballots have to be notarized. We have to know who they are. And then they have to be in by Election Day. So they’re all counted, and then when the polls close at 7, we drop all the absentee and early votes counted. Bam, you know what they are at 7:01.

It is weird that in a swing state, in a certain county, it takes them a month to count the votes. So rightly, you should be questioning some of these things. But Oklahoma does it the right way, and those are the things that I’m responsible for. But, yeah, I trust our election process.

AP: But if you were to look at those vote swings, do you trust governors of those states to look at that as opposed to Washington?

STITT: 100%. I don’t think we should federalize that. Because then you’ve got a pendulum swing. What about the next guy gets in office and the next guy and the next guy? The system that we have with 50 different states is the right system.

Now, the Save America Act, making sure that we know who’s voting, I think that’s a very legitimate thing to do.

AP: You pushed back against the president when he wanted to exclude two Democratic governors from a White House meeting. The president had some words for you as well at the time. As a Republican, how do you disagree with the president?

STITT: All I simply said was, “Hey, we can’t call this a National Governors Association meeting if you’re not going to have all the governors there.” And so, to President Donald Trump’s credit, he said, and I think he was getting bad information from staff at the time, but, yes, we talked, and all the governors were invited to the business meeting. He excluded a couple of governors from the dinner. But that’s all I basically said. I didn’t want to get on the bad side of the president. But we have a good working relationship.

I’m trying to do what’s best for Oklahoma. In that case, I was representing the National Governors Association.

AP: It sometimes seems that when Republicans push back against the president, it’s often when they’re leaving office. Should there be more open and frequent disagreement?

STITT: Well, I mean, sure. If there’s something that we fundamentally think is going to be bad for our country, we all should say something. Every citizen, regardless if you’re a Republican or a Democrat, we should say, “Hey, that’s the wrong approach.”

AP: How do we bring down the temperature in politics?

STITT: I think one of the reasons the temperature’s so hard, so loud and divisive, is because of this one-size-fits-all, huge federal government.

Then we want whatever idea we have, then we want everybody to do it across the country. And that is not how our founders set it up. They thought that New York was different from Delaware, different from Virginia and South Carolina and Maryland.

And that’s OK, and that’s what I tell people. Hey, Minnesota’s elected Gov. Tim Walz. That’s OK. Why does that bother me in Oklahoma? Why do I care what Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s doing in New York City? It shouldn’t affect me.

But politics is becoming like, if Kamala Harris wins, she’s going to try to make Oklahoma like California. We don’t want to be like California. And so I think if we can bring that temperature down and say, “Hey, it’s OK that the states are different and they have different values and philosophies.”

AP: What do you see as the future of the Republican Party?

STITT: I hope we get back to the fiscal piece of our party. Like in 1994, when Newt Gingrich came in with the Contract with America, and President Bill Clinton was in office, we balanced a budget. Now, Congress won’t even vote on a budget — it’s continuing resolutions. And our Founding Fathers would just be like, “What is this? What do you mean they don’t ever vote on the budget? That’s all their job is.”

AP: Do you plan on running for anything again, maybe national office?

STITT: I’m just going to finish my job as governor and plan on going back to the private sector, and we’ll see what happens in the future.

news.title: Chicago Democratic Socialist Meetings to Teach Governance, Vote on New Party and Presidential Candidate
news.text:
The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), who have defeated several Democrat incumbents this election cycle, will be hosting their “Socialists Summit” this weekend, July 31-August 2, in Chicago. At this summit, the DSA will offer socialist organizing training to its participants, including on “Governing as Socialists” and on “Building to a General Strike.” This event will include a surprise keynote speaker, and all those who attend will have to submit a negative COVID test.

At the same time, the Young Democratic Socialists of America (YDSA), “the youth and student section of the Democratic Socialists of America,” are holding their convention, where they will be voting on whether to field and endorse a presidential candidate in 2028, as well as on whether to call for a new party outside the Democratic Party.

The YDSA will be voting on several resolutions at the convention, most of them having to do with forming and supporting labor movements and other Socialist organizations. One of the more noteworthy resolutions is resolution 18, titled “Preparing for a Class-Struggle 2028 Presidential election.” If adopted, the YDSA would move to create an infrastructure to support a potential DSA candidate for president.

In one of the resolution’s preambles, the YDSA criticize Kamala Harris for being too rightwing. In another, it characterizes the Democratic Party as “class-collaborationist,” and states its aim to “build an independent, socialist political force fighting to win a majority of society over to our politics,” implying that it believes a Democratic Socialist could win a majority of Americans over to the movement, despite the party’s many radical proposals. 

If DSA were to advance a presidential candidate, the YDSA would not “hide, minimize, or alter [their] platform and vision” for the sake of appealing to more voters. It also promises to criticize and differentiate itself from the DSA candidate, if it deems necessary, a strategy quite uncommon in presidential elections.

The young Democratic Socialists will also be voting on a resolution (23) to call for the creation a new Socialist party in America:

“Let it be resolved that the signatories of this resolution motion for the creation of a Socialist Party independent of the Democratic Party; one which should be fit for competing in state & local races no later than 2028, a roadmap to the accomplishment of which DSA/YDSA invites, as equals, other anti-capitalist, anti-imperialist & anti-Zionist associations or parties to participate in drafting.”

According to the resolution, the DSA would invite other current leftwing organizations, including the Working Families Party, the Communist Party USA, and the Green Party into a new party, a “Socialist Party.” The resolution does not explicitly rule out contesting Democrat primaries, as the DSA has been winning many of them. It does, however, signal opposition to working within the Democratic Party framework, and accuses the Democrats of favoring “Fascists” to Socialists, while indicating a belief that Socialist candidates could win apart from the Democratic Party:

“Whereas the recent successes of openly socialist candidates (DSA or otherwise) in state & local elections have demonstrated clearly the political appetite for a Socialist Party independent of the Democratic Party.”…“Whereas the liberal capitalists in control of the Democratic Party would sooner do battle with socialists than with fascists.”

The Democratic Socialists of America currently have negative net favorability. According to a July 15th Echelon insights poll, 25% of Americans have a very or somewhat favorable view of the DSA, while 46% have a very or somewhat unfavorable view. A CNN poll suggests that around one in three Democrats identify as Democratic Socialists, though it is unclear whether they would leave the Democratic Party to vote for hypothetical Socialist Party candidates.

news.title: New York sues Kalshi, says its prediction markets are illegal gambling
news.text: New York’s attorney general sued prediction market operator Kalshi on Friday, claiming that its platform violates state laws against illegal gambling. In a petition filed in a state court in Manhattan, Attorney General Letitia James said Kalshi failed to obtain a New York State Gaming Commission license to operate its platform, where people trade based on the predicted outcomes of sports, elections and other events. The attorney general said such platforms can encourage problem gambling, including by people under age 21, and endanger people’s financial, emotional and physical health. She filed similar petitions in April against two other prediction market operators, Coinbase Financial Markets and Gemini Titan, saying all three companies’ so-called event contracts were “quintessentially” gambling. “New York’s gambling laws protect children from underage betting and help combat gambling addiction,” James said in a statement. “No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple.” CFTC Challenges New York Prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket have soared in popularity since the 2024 U.S. presidential election, when they fared better than pollsters in predicting Republican Donald Trump’s victory over Democrat Kamala Harris. Their growth has sparked a flurry of lawsuits and countersuits over the authority of individual U.S. states, rather than the federal government, to regulate the industry. The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission has claimed exclusive oversight and challenged regulatory activity in at least nine states including New York, which it sued in April. “It’s sad to see this type of political theater from the leadership in our own state,” New York-based Kalshi said in a statement. “States can’t just shut down a federally licensed exchange.” Less than one hour before New York sued Kalshi, the CFTC filed an “emergency” motion in Manhattan federal court to stop the state’s enforcement activity, calling it “overreach” that would irreparably harm the agency and markets it regulates. The CFTC filing followed Wednesday’s rejection by the federal appeals court in Manhattan of Kalshi‘s request to avoid being subjected to New York’s gambling laws, while it appeals U.S. District Judge Analisa Torres’ refusal on July 8 to issue an injunction against the state. Kalshi had preemptively sued New York last October to block enforcement. According to New York’s petition, Kalshi‘s prediction markets are gambling because people can wager on events whose outcomes they don’t control, such as who will win the Super Bowl or the reality TV show “Big Brother.” New York also objected to Kalshi letting 18- to 20-year-olds use its platform, despite a minimum age of 21 under state law for mobile sports betting. “Kalshi has chosen to ignore New York’s gaming laws, which exist to protect consumers, prevent problematic gambling, deliver funding for critical public services, and ensure that every company plays by the same rules,” New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement. “This choice has consequences.” At least four states — Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada and Washington — have won court orders restricting Kalshi‘s activities. In refusing to stop potential New York enforcement activity, Torres found the state’s interests in preventing gambling addiction, preserving the integrity of sports, and avoiding ​a proliferation of unregulated contracts “heavily” outweighed Kalshi‘s interests in ensuring the primacy of federal law and avoiding “intractable” technology issues for customers. New York’s lawsuit seeks a halt to Kalshi‘s alleged unlawful conduct, the forfeiture of illegal gains, civil fines equal to triple those gains, and restitution to customers.

news.title: Will Black voters go with the establishment? Michigan’s Senate primary tests it.
news.text:
DETROIT — In a Michigan Democratic primary, the path to a majority usually runs through the same rooms: Black churches, and the older voters who fill their pews and make up the party’s most reliable base. Which is why Rep. Haley Stevens has spent the past month working those rooms harder than any others.

Eight times this month, she has carried her Senate campaign into a predominantly Black church and made essentially the same case: her roots growing up in the Detroit suburbs, her endorsements from members of the Congressional Black Caucus and her ties to President Barack Obama, for whom she worked on the U.S. Auto Rescue Task Force in 2009. 

“President Obama, our 44th president of the United States, I worked on that campaign and I saw him get elected, and I put up my hand to serve in that administration,” Stevens told the congregation at New Hope Baptist Church in Ann Arbor during a recent stop. Her Obama ties have been a focus of campaign mailers and more than a million dollars in ad buys paid for on her behalf by outside political action committees.

That effort reflects a deliberate bet on the voters she needs most — the constituency that could decide her competitive primary against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed on Tuesday. It also underscores the danger she faces. El-Sayed, a public health expert and 2018 candidate for governor, has built his campaign around the roughly $60 million that PACs have spent to boost Stevens — above all, the more than $30 million spent on ads by a group aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying organization.

For now, those voters appear to be holding firm. Interviews with roughly a dozen Black voters, party leaders and elected officials across Michigan suggest the state’s most active Black voters — those older than 55 — are less troubled by that outside money, helping explain why Stevens has concentrated her closing weeks on turning them out.

“I don’t think it matters as much as really proving to me that she’s doing what she says she’s going to do to represent the people,” said Darius Randolph, 65, of Ypsilanti, after Stevens spoke at New Hope Baptist.

But beneath that stability runs a set of fault lines that could reshape the coalition for years — over generation, over Gaza, and over what the Democratic Party owes voters who have never stopped showing up for it. And for some Black Michiganders, tensions still linger from the state’s 2024 “Uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to vote “uncommitted” rather than for Joe Biden in that year's primary to protest U.S. support for Israel's military campaign in Gaza. That history — along with the false perception that El-Sayed was among the Uncommitted activists who opposed Kamala Harris in the general election — could also help Stevens, several Black Democrats acknowledged to MS NOW.

Black voters are not a monolith, and El-Sayed’s allies argue his progressive platform will play well with younger voters of every race. The divide runs through the institutions that have weighed in: The Congressional Black Caucus endorsed Stevens, but at least five of its younger, progressive members have broken to back El-Sayed. The Michigan Council of COGIC Bishops endorsed Stevens; El-Sayed’s website touts endorsements from two church leaders tied to the group.

El-Sayed’s path on Tuesday runs through those divisions — peeling off enough Black voters to deny Stevens a win, much as Sen. Bernie Sanders, an El-Sayed backer, did in Michigan’s 2016 presidential primary, when he carried the state while winning roughly 28% of the Black vote. For Stevens, victory means running up turnout among Democrats’ most reliable voters in places like Wayne County — where she has spent the bulk of her campaign’s final weeks— and Detroit, the largest Black-majority city in the country.

Either way, allies of both candidates said the race could turn on Black voters, a group that makes up roughly a quarter of the state's Democratic electorate.

The ghost of 2024

When Stevens opened a campaign event last weekend at a Teamsters hall in Detroit alongside Rep. Jim Clyburn, the surprise she had planned for her mostly older crowd was an endorsement from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer — one of the few, Williams said, that carries weight with Black voters.

The surprise she hadn’t planned for was a now-viral clip of a supporter, Farmington school board member Angie Smith, making explicitly Islamophobic remarks as she explained her opposition to El-Sayed.

“We need some of us that can represent all of us and not just one race but all races,” Smith told reporter Sam Robinson of the Michigan Chronicle. “Don’t come out speaking only Arabic, don’t come out with your Arabic music on. Represent everyone.” (El-Sayed, who is Muslim and has Egyptian ancestry, campaigns in English and has not been known to play Arabic music at rallies.)

The comments drew wide condemnation, including from Stevens. But voters and party leaders said they reflected rising tensions between Black and Arab residents rooted in the Uncommitted movement, an effort that sought to deny Democrats votes due to the Biden administration’s funding support for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

“My people died for the right to vote, and y’all just talk about being ‘uncommitted,’" Williams, who endorsed Stevens, told MS NOW. “Donald Trump won [Michigan in 2024] by 80,000 votes, and that’s where the tension lies.”

To El-Sayed’s backers, that resentment has curdled into something broader. “A lot of the African American community are trying to put a face on the Uncommitted movement,” said Tomena Rawls, a Michigan Democratic Party official backing El-Sayed. The dynamic, she said, is affecting not only El-Sayed, but also Rep. Rashida Tlaib, who is seeking re-election, and state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, who was a co-founder of the Uncommitted effort.

Rawls and other El-Sayed supporters argue the movement was not responsible for Harris's defeat across all eight swing states in 2024. But memories of the movement — including event disruptions and online attacks that some in the movement aimed at Harris — won't fade easily, especially as the United Democracy Project, an AIPAC-aligned group, pours millions into advertisements seeking to remind Michiganders of El-Sayed’s support of Uncommitted, though he later endorsed Harris.

“It’s just that when they voted for Jill Stein, and you had some content creators saying awful, awful things about Kamala Harris and how they, you know, they would vote for the devil instead of voting for her and everything. That turned off a lot of Black folks, especially the 92%,” Rawls, the El-Sayed backer, said, referencing the 92% of Black women that backed Harris in 2024.

Williams told MS NOW that he’d support El-Sayed in the general election should he defeat Stevens on Tuesday, and expects most Black voters would do the same. But in a primary defined by the candidates’ positions on U.S. military aid to Israel, Williams cautioned that the war in Gaza may not resonate as deeply with Black voters.

“I feel for folks. I don’t want to see people die [in the Middle East], but my people are dying every day in the hood from gun violence, from not having … the great education they need to succeed and survive in this community,” Williams said. “So I’m sympathetic, but it’s not my issue.”

The Generation Gap

“I was proud to work with Obama,” Stevens jubilantly told a group of seniors at the Summer Sizzler, an event on Tuesday hosted by Detroit Councilwoman Mary Waters. Stevens’ remarks and literature, and the PACs backing her, have worked to sear that Obama-era work into voters’ memories, even though the former president has withheld an endorsement in the primary. Interviews with several Black voters suggest it is working — at least with older voters.

“I think that her relationships are important. I think that she was supportive of President Obama when he was in office and his initiatives, especially as they involved what it took to save our industries here in Michigan,” said Rev. Diane Smith of Ypsilanti.

But El-Sayed’s supporters say the Obama focus only confirms the fault line they already see in the race: Older Black voters lean toward Stevens. They doubt it will land with the younger voters El-Sayed has aggressively courted.

“There are a fair number of younger Black and brown people — especially younger black people, younger black men — who don't really give a fuck about what Obama thinks,” said Pontiac City Councilperson Mikal Goodman, the former chair of the Detroit chapter of the Democratic Socialist of America.

Warren Evans, the Wayne County executive who appointed El-Sayed as county health director in 2022, suggested older Black support for Stevens reflects fear of a Republican trifecta in Washington that has targeted Black voting rights and driven up costs.

“Their feeling is the Republican Party has gone way overboard, and that means that we need a traditional conservative, strong Democrat,” said Evans, who’s endorsed El-Sayed. “I don’t necessarily see the correlation the same way they do, but I do see a significant younger — probably more progressive — group of African Americans who don’t see it that way.” 

In 2016, Sanders narrowly beat Hillary Clinton in Michigan’s Democratic presidential primary with an electorate that included nearly 60% of voters under 45 and less than a third — 28% — of Black voters. Goodman expects El-Sayed to assemble something similar, and to overperform among older Black voters drawn to his focus on lowering health care costs and steering tax dollars away from foreign wars.

“This is not to say that Haley’s not going to, you know, possibly still end up winning the majority of the older black vote, but a lot of those older Black women, older Black men, these churchgoers who would have been all for Haley three to four years ago, enough of them are starting to break off,” Goodman said. 

The affordability test

Whatever the outcome Tuesday, Black leaders said mobilizing Black Michiganders will be crucial to Democrats' hopes of beating Mike Rogers in November. Rogers, who narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024, has Trump's endorsement and appeared with him Monday at a rally in Milford.

Supporters of both Stevens and El-Sayed told MS NOW defeating Rogers will require a laser focus on affordability and economic prosperity. According to a 2025 study, Black Michiganders have a higher unemployment rate and lower household income than the statewide average. Meanwhile, the poverty rate in Black-majority cities is more than twice the overall state level.

Meeting those numbers with concrete policy, party leaders say, is the price of turning out Black voters.

“Black folks are yearning. They want prosperity, man. They’re tired. We're tired, man,” said Williams, the Black Caucus chair.
